data.title: Middle East Eye: Shobeiri Zanjani: The quiet ayatollah who bridged Iran’s political divide
data.author: MEE correspondent
data.summary:
Shobeiri Zanjani: The quiet ayatollah who bridged Iran’s political divide
Submitted by
MEE correspondent
on
Mon, 09/28/2026 - 12:38
Grand Ayatollah Mousa Shobeiri Zanjani passed away on 20 September at the age of 98
Grand Ayatollah Mousa Shobeiri Zanjani was a highly respected and influential religious figure across Iran's political spectrum (X)
Off
When Grand Ayatollah Mousa Shobeiri Zanjani died at 98 on 20 September, he left behind a rare position in Iran’s religious establishment: a cleric who kept his distance from political power, yet whose influence reached across the Islamic Republic’s deepest political divides.
His students included former reformist President Mohammad Khatami and, according to a source in the Qom Seminary, Mojtaba Khamenei, the current supreme leader. For decades, politicians and clerics on opposing sides of Iran’s political spectrum turned to Shobeiri because his authority rested outside politics.
That independence made him an important figure at moments when Iran’s political and religious establishments collided.
Shobeiri was one of seven senior clerics identified by the Society of Seminary Scholars of Qom in the 1990s as qualified to be followed as a grand ayatollah and serve as a marja, or religious authority.
The ayatollah belonged to a strand of the Iranian clergy that believed clerics should not directly enter politics.
They are often described as “traditional” clerics, a group that includes Ayatollah Vahid Khorasani, another highly respected figure in the seminary establishment. Both men have largely stayed outside of the Islamic Republic's factional politics.
Traditional clerics tend to see their role primarily as preserving the independence of the seminaries from the state, maintaining the institution of marjaʿiyyah – the system of senior religious authorities whom believers may follow for guidance on matters of Islamic law – and addressing religious and social affairs rather than directly participating in political power.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Vietnam taught America the limits of its power. Hormuz is teaching it again
data.author: Sami Al-Arian
data.summary:
Vietnam taught America the limits of its power. Hormuz is teaching it again
Submitted by
Sami Al-Arian
on
Tue, 09/29/2026 - 17:43
Washington believed the 1991 Gulf War had overcome the 'Vietnam Syndrome'. Seven months of bombing and blockade against Iran have brought it back
Vessels sit in the Strait of Hormuz near Bandar Abbas, Iran, on 28 September 2026, a week after commercial crossings of the strait fell to two in a single day (Amirhosein Khorgooi/ISNA/WANA via Reuters)
On
On 22 September, only two commercial vessels crossed the Strait of Hormuz. A narrow choke point that normally handles a fifth of the world's daily oil supply, as well as a fifth of globally traded liquefied natural gas, sits almost silent under the watch of multibillion-dollar American warships that cannot convince commercial insurers to risk even a handful of tankers.
Washington can still destroy almost anything it targets across the Middle East, but whether that destruction can buy the political outcome it wants is a vastly different question.
Seven months into the war against Iran that began on 28 February 2026, Washington has cycled through three strategies of coercion: massive aerial bombardment, economic strangulation through a naval blockade and direct tit-for-tat escalation. None restored normal passage through the strait.
The US military can dominate the skies, sink ships and eliminate political and military leaders, yet it remains unable to compel Tehran to accept its terms.
Vietnam, the Gulf War of 1991 and the current war in the Gulf belong to different eras and involve radically different adversaries that cannot be mechanically equated, yet each tells us something important about the limits and reach of American power.
The "Vietnam Syndrome" was more than a domestic aversion to casualties. It was a crisis of confidence in the efficacy, morality and political utility of American military power.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli attacks caused 70 percent of recorded Gaza deaths in 2025
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Israeli attacks caused 70 percent of recorded Gaza deaths in 2025
Israeli forces’ attacks caused 70.1 percent of the 24,650 deaths the Palestinian health ministry in Gaza registered last year, according to its first official mortality report since 2022.
The under-five mortality rate more than doubled, reaching 33.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2025 compared with 13.6 in 2022. Excluding war deaths, the ministry put the rate at 15.8.
Heart disease accounted for 7.7 percent of recorded deaths, making it the second-largest cause. Males represented 73.4 percent of those who died and females 26.6 percent.
Gaza City accounted for the largest share of deaths at 37.3 percent. The North Gaza governorate followed with 20.2 percent, ahead of Khan Younis at 19.5 percent, the Middle Area at 12.3 percent and Rafah at 10.7 percent.

data.title: Middle East Eye: ‘We are stuck here’: In cramped shelters, Lebanon’s displaced dream of their villages
data.author: Gergana Krasteva
data.summary:
‘We are stuck here’: In cramped shelters, Lebanon’s displaced dream of their villages
Submitted by
Gergana Krasteva
on
Mon, 09/14/2026 - 15:21
Six months after the war, Lebanese families still live in limbo with no homes to return to
Hassan Bisher, 33, a taxi driver in Nabatieh, speaks about losing his home in the town of Kfar Tebnit (Gergana Krasteva/MEE)
Off
A 72-hour-old newborn is laid to sleep on a thin, worn-out mattress on the floor of a school in Sidon, south Lebanon, his first days unfolding in a classroom-turned-shelter.
His mother, Hala Loubany, 29, has just had a C-section. She watches over the baby boy, one hand resting protectively over the throbbing scar on her stomach.
Next to them, separated by a shelf crammed with canned food and clothes, an elderly man is preparing lunch for himself and his wife.
Three families live in this classroom, their few belongings packed into corners as they wait to return to Nabatieh’s southern district.
Israel's bombardment has destroyed infrastructure, including thousands of homes, across south Lebanon, with more than two dozen Lebanese border towns and villages razed. Tens of thousands of people have been displaced.
“Hala’s water broke here, in the school, so she was taken to the hospital at the last minute,” her father, Ali Mahmoud Loubany, told Middle East Eye. “It was an emergency so doctors performed a C-section.”
Hala was six months pregnant when she, her husband, their two sons, aged six and one, and her father fled Nabatieh. The school in Sidon is the second shelter they have been forced to seek refuge in.
Directly opposite the classroom is the only women’s bathroom on the floor. Families have to schedule showers in the three laminate stalls and wash their clothes in the shallow sinks.
For Hala, who is still recovering from surgery, poor sanitation is a major source of anxiety, as she worries about her wound becoming infected.
'No one by our side'
At 54, her father says he is “sick” of his family being displaced

data.title: Middle East Eye: Morocco appoints its first woman prime minister
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Morocco appoints its first woman prime minister
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 09/30/2026 - 11:05
Named by the king after her party’s victory in last week’s legislative elections, Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri now faces numerous challenges
Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, Morocco's newly appointed head of government, arrives for a meeting in Rabat on 29 September 2026 (Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP)
Off
Morocco’s King Mohammed VI has appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as head of the government, one week after her party won the legislative elections.
For the first time in its history, the North African kingdom will be led by a woman.
“This is truly a historic moment,” El Mansouri told public media after her audience at the royal palace.
“For the first time in our country’s history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government. This is not only a source of pride for me, but for all Moroccan women,” she added.
At 50, the lawyer becomes the thrid woman in the Arab world to reach this position, after Najla Bouden and Sarra Zaafarani in Tunisia.
El Mansouri had already made history by becoming, at just 33, the first woman to serve as mayor of the tourist city of Marrakesh in 2009 - a position she currently holds for a second term since 2021.
She had also made her mark during the 2023 earthquake, visiting affected communities repeatedly.
Currently the national coordinator of the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), outgoing minister of housing and spatial planning, and a newly re-elected MP, El Mansouri had been widely tipped for the role in recent weeks.
However, without an absolute majority, the new prime minister will now need to form a coalition government for the next five years ahead of the 9 October parliamentary session.
A centre-right party, the PAM - part of the outgoing governing coalition - secured 97 of the 395 seats in the House of Representatives in an election marked by a turnout of just 38 percent, the lowest in nearly two decades.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Labour minister: British Muslims haven't always been heard but Burnham will change that
data.author: Imran Mulla
data.summary:
Labour minister: British Muslims haven't always been heard but Burnham will change that
Submitted by
Imran Mulla
on
Wed, 09/30/2026 - 10:58
A reception at the Labour conference showed the government has turned a new page on engagement with Muslim civil society
The cake is cut at Equi's reception on Sunday evening at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool. (Imran Mulla/MEE)
Off
Not too long ago, British Muslim civil society barely engaged with the government. This was less because of British Muslims than because of the government itself.
The Conservative Party, who were ousted in 2024, made no particular attempt - especially after 2020 - to even appear to engage with mainstream Muslim organisations.
Fast forward to today and the situation has fundamentally transformed.
At the Labour Party conference, the widespread feeling among Muslims - both MPs and party members - was that things are looking up. "A new hope," as one parliamentary advisor called it, referencing Star Wars.
The reason: Andy Burnham.
Engagement with Muslims did improve under Keir Starmer's Labour government, but the relationship remained fraught: large numbers of Muslim voters abandoned Labour over its support for Israel during the Gaza genocide.
Under new Prime Minister Burnham, however, relations are better than they have been for decades.
This was in clear evidence at an event at the Hilton hotel at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool on Sunday evening.
Equi, a Muslim think tank, was celebrating its two-year anniversary.
The room was packed with representatives of Muslim civil society organisations, Labour members and several MPs.
"I had the privilege of being invited to the Foreign Office by the foreign secretary the day before he made the announcement on sanctions, on the Middle East," said Professor Javed Khan, Equi's director.

data.author: Laura O'Connor

Gaza students take Ireland to court over visa refusals
Submitted by
Laura O'Connor
on
Wed, 09/30/2026 - 11:50
A legal team says the justice minister's decision is irrational and discriminatory, with 26 more cases in the pipeline
Displaced Palestinian university students hold up signs during a rally calling for easier travel to pursue education outside the Gaza Strip, in Gaza City on 20 April 2026 (AFP)
Off
When Hazem Faris, 19, received a full scholarship to study Computer Science at Ireland’s South East Technological University, it felt like he had the opportunity to “achieve a dream”, he said.
Faris lives in Gaza, and since 2023 he and his family have been forced to evacuate their homes eight times. However, when the Irish government denied Faris’s visa, his dreams became impossible.
Faris is one of the at least 103 Palestinian students who have had their visas rejected in Ireland this year, with visa approval rates dropping from 83.8 percent in 2025 to just 27.5 percent this year.
Last week, a team of lawyers challenged Minister of Justice Jim O’Callaghan’s refusal, asking him to reverse the decision.
The instructed barristers are Blinne Ni Ghralaigh, who represented South Africa at the International Court of Justice in its genocide case against Israel, and Eamonn Dornan. The solicitors include Sinead Marmion and Alannah Faulkner, alongside several junior counsel.
The legal action was launched last week, beginning with the case of Palestinian student Hafez Alrayyes, from Gaza.
Marmion said a further 26 cases are in the pipeline. “I think the other side is worried about the size and speed of [the case],” Marmion told Middle East Eye.
Marmion and her colleagues made an administrative appearance in the High Court on Tuesday, confirming that evidence and legal submissions will be with the court this week.
“We are back in court to see how ready the other side is with a view to expedite a hearing next week, probably Monday,” she said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israel-bound plane lands in Saudi Arabia after pilot allegedly tries to crash it
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Israel-bound plane lands in Saudi Arabia after pilot allegedly tries to crash it
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Wed, 09/30/2026 - 08:12
Witnesses say passengers overpowered one crew member and regained control as the aircraft rapidly lost altitude
A Flydubai Boeing 737 MAX 8 performs a display flight at Al-Maktoum International Airport during the Dubai Airshow on 17 November 2025 (Giuseppe Cacace/AFP)
Off
An Israel-bound flight made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after its co-pilot allegedly attempted to crash the plane.
The Flydubai flight was travelling from Dubai to Ben Gurion Airport with 180 passengers on board, most of them Israeli.
About an hour before its scheduled arrival, the plane began a steep descent, dropping from 34,000 feet (10,363 metres) to 16,000 feet (4876.8 metres) in less than two minutes.
It eventually landed safely in Tabuk, in northwestern Saudi Arabia.
The company that operates Tabuk airport said both the captain and first officer were injured and taken to hospital.
Israeli media later cited witnesses as saying that the co-pilot stabbed the captain, attempted to hijack the plane and tried to crash it.
Passengers reportedly broke into the cockpit, intervened to stop the descent and regained control of the plane.
Images released from the flight appeared to show one pilot restrained and the other covered in blood.
Israeli media reported that authorities were treating the incident as a suspected “terror attack”, alleging that the co-pilot was of Omani origin.
Middle East Eye could not independently verify the reports.
There is no indication at this stage that the incident was directed by any organisation or state, according to Israeli media.
A senior Israeli official told Channel 12 that a “severe disaster was prevented”.
Israeli investigation
